messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Valentina Cruz is a 38-year-old single woman of Colombian descent who works on the assembly line at a food packaging factory in a mid-sized Midwestern city. She was referred for psychological assessment following a PCL-5 score of 72, and she presented to her first session visibly guarded, speaking quietly and choosing her words with great care, as though she feared that saying certain things aloud might make them more real.

Approximately fourteen months ago, Valentina received a phone call in the middle of her overnight shift at the factory. The call came from her younger brother, who told her that their mother had collapsed at home and that by the time the ambulance arrived, she was already gone — a massive cardiac event, without warning, without any chance for Valentina to be present or to say goodbye. Valentina had spoken to her mother just hours earlier. They had talked about nothing in particular: what to cook on Sunday, whether Valentina's niece was sleeping better. The ordinariness of that last conversation became, over the following months, one of the most unbearable facts of her life. She had not known it was the last one. She had not treated it as if it mattered enough.

In the weeks after the death, Valentina began to notice that certain sounds and situations reached inside her and pulled her back to that night. The wail of an ambulance siren — unavoidable at the factory, which sits near a busy arterial road — would stop her mid-motion at the conveyor belt, her hands going still, her chest tightening as the sound carried her back to imagining the vehicle that had come too late for her mother. Funerals, cemeteries, even a colleague mentioning that she had lost a relative — any of these would flood Valentina with the same raw, unprocessed grief as if the death had just occurred. It was in the immediate aftermath of these moments that Valentina found herself doing the things she had come to rely on, even knowing they did not help: she would go over the night again and again in her mind, searching for the detail she had missed, the sign she should have seen, the phone call she should have made earlier that week. She would text her brother or her closest friend seeking confirmation that she was not losing her mind, that she was going to be okay. These responses were automatic, almost reflexive — the triggers arrived and the rumination and reassurance-seeking followed as surely as an exhale follows an inhale.

But the relief those strategies offered was short-lived, and over months their costs accumulated. The relentless overanalysing, rather than producing the understanding Valentina craved, only deepened her sense that something essential had been permanently broken. The more she sought reassurance, the more she came to feel that no answer anyone gave her was sufficient — which in turn confirmed her growing conviction that she had been destroyed by what had happened, that the woman who had laughed easily and looked forward to things was simply gone. She had come to believe that she no longer belonged anywhere: not at the factory, where she moved through her shifts like a ghost; not at family gatherings, where everyone else seemed to be finding their way back to ordinary life while she remained stranded. These beliefs — that her life had been destroyed, that she was permanently miserable, that she fit nowhere — did not remain static. They became the lens through which she encountered the world, so that when a siren sounded or a coworker mentioned a funeral, the trigger landed not just as a sensory jolt but as confirmation of everything she already feared about herself and her future.

Valentina had spent over a year avoiding anything that reminded her of loss — she had stopped attending church, declined a cousin's wedding because the family gathering felt too close to grief, and muted words like "funeral" or "cemetery" in her social media feeds — yet the world kept finding ways through. What finally brought her to seek help was a moment at work three weeks ago when a siren passed and she began crying at her station and could not stop. A supervisor noticed. Valentina, who had always prided herself on her composure, found that the humiliation of that moment was less frightening than the thought of another year lived this way. What she most hopes for, she said quietly at the end of the intake, is to remember her mother without it feeling like dying herself.
